item.title: European startup OSMOS X begins bodyguard satellite development to address European capability gap
item.description: LONDON – A consortium of European space companies and research institutions has kicked off development of a dual-use orbital capture demonstrator aiming to address the European technology gap in space control and orbital defense. The project could pave the way for a fleet of orbital bodyguards — guardian satellites that would be stationed near critical European assets in space — amid growing geopolitical tensions.

item.title: Is faster and cheaper really better for NASA science?
item.description: Since NASA Administrator Dan Goldin introduced the concept of “faster, better, cheaper” to the agency in the 1990s, a debate has raged: Can smaller missions, which are faster and less expensive to develop but carry a higher risk of failure, be as effective as larger flagship missions, which have been prone to major cost and schedule overruns?

item.title: Small nations don’t need a Space Force. They need the right space organization.
item.description: The establishment of the United States Space Force, China’s Aerospace Force and France’s Space Command has prompted political and military leaders to consider creating similar organizations. For small and medium-sized states, that temptation is a trap. Recognizing space as a warfighting domain compels smaller states to develop military space organizations — but not as national symbols. The main limitations are the strategic position of these small states and their budgets to build and sustain such organizations. For small and medium-sized states, creating a military space organization involves an opportunity cost. Resources could alternatively be allocated to building more combat units or acquiring additional tanks, aircraft and ships. On the other hand, a smaller military space organization may be a force multiplier to help the mission.
